config.title: Build a sortable and filterable table

intro.title: Build a sortable and filterable table
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a dynamic table that displays data which can be sorted by column and filtered by a search term. You will learn how to manage and transform data arrays using JavaScript's built-in array methods like `sort()` and `filter()`. The core concepts involve handling state for the data and user inputs, and writing event handler functions to update the table. You'll create this interactive feature using plain JavaScript, HTML for structure, and CSS for basic styling, all within a single JavaScript file context.
intro.usecase: Sortable and filterable tables are essential UI components in data-intensive applications like e-commerce dashboards, admin panels, and analytics tools. For example, product managers use them to sort customer data by date or filter support tickets by status in platforms like Shopify or Zendesk. Developers implement these features to help users efficiently navigate large datasets, such as filtering inventory by category or sorting financial records by amount. Mastering this pattern enables you to build professional-grade interfaces that handle real-world data exploration needs.

objectives: Construct a table structure with HTML and populate it with JavaScript data
Implement sorting functionality for table columns with click handlers
Apply filtering logic to display rows based on user input criteria
Initialize and manipulate state variables to track sort order and filter values
Bind event listeners to UI controls for interactive table operations
Render dynamic table updates based on current sort and filter conditions
Integrate sorting and filtering features into a cohesive user interface

steps.title: Initialize table data state
steps.instruction: Inside the App component, use the useState hook to create a state variable named 'data' and initialize it with a sample array of objects representing table rows.
steps.hint: Call useState with an array of objects, each containing properties like id, name, age, etc. Assign the returned array to a variable named 'data'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component now has a 'data' state variable initialized with sample data, ready to be displayed in a table.
successCriteria: The useState hook is called inside the App component, creating a 'data' state variable initialized with an array of objects.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using useState correctly. Check that you've named the variable 'data' and initialized it with an array of objects.
steps.feedbackWrong: The state initialization isn't quite right. Remember to use useState inside the component, name the variable 'data', and provide an initial array of objects.

steps.title: Initialize filtered data state
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, create a second state variable called 'filteredData' using useState. Initialize it with the same array as your 'tableData' state.
steps.hint: You'll need to call useState again with the initial value. This state will hold the data that gets displayed after filtering and sorting.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: another state variable
const [filteredItems, setFilteredItems] = useState(initialItems);
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component will have two state variables: 'tableData' for the original data and 'filteredData' for the display data.
successCriteria: A 'filteredData' state variable is declared with useState and initialized with the same array as 'tableData'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure filteredData is initialized with the same array as tableData.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've properly declared filteredData using useState with the correct initial value.

steps.title: Initialize sort configuration state
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, use useState to create a state variable called 'sortConfig' that will track the current sort column and direction. Initialize it as an object with 'key' set to null and 'direction' set to null.
steps.hint: You'll need to call useState with an initial value of { key: null, direction: null }.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: state for tracking sort configuration
const [sortConfig, setSortConfig] = useState({ key: null, direction: null });
steps.expectedOutcome: After this step, you'll have a sortConfig state variable that can track which column is being sorted and in which direction (ascending/descending).
successCriteria: The sortConfig state is declared with useState, initialized as an object with key and direction properties set to null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're creating a state variable called 'sortConfig' with the correct initial structure: an object with 'key' and 'direction' properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: create a state variable called 'sortConfig' using useState, initialized as { key: null, direction: null }.

steps.title: Define the handleSort function
steps.instruction: Inside your component, define a function named handleSort that takes a key parameter (like 'name' or 'age'). This function will eventually handle sorting logic.
steps.hint: Create a function that accepts a parameter and has an empty body for now. You'll add the sorting logic in later steps.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a handleSort function defined inside your component that accepts a key parameter.
successCriteria: A function named handleSort is defined inside the component and accepts one parameter.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've defined a function named handleSort that accepts a parameter (like 'key').
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleSort function isn't defined correctly. Check that you've created a function with the right name and parameter inside your component.

steps.title: Define the handleFilter function
steps.instruction: Define a function named handleFilter that takes a filterValue parameter and updates the filteredData state with the filtered results from tableData.
steps.hint: Inside the function, use the filterValue to filter tableData (e.g., by checking if the name includes the filterValue), then call setFilteredData with the filtered array.
steps.expectedOutcome: A handleFilter function is defined that filters tableData based on a filterValue and updates filteredData state.
successCriteria: The handleFilter function is defined, takes a filterValue parameter, filters tableData (e.g., by checking if name includes filterValue), and calls setFilteredData with the filtered results.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started defining handleFilter, but make sure it takes a filterValue parameter, filters tableData, and calls setFilteredData with the results.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleFilter function is not correctly defined. It should take a filterValue parameter, filter tableData based on that value, and update filteredData state.

steps.title: Add table container and filter input
steps.instruction: Inside the component's return statement, add a <div> container after the heading. Inside this container, add an <input> element for filtering with placeholder text 'Filter by name...' and an empty <table> element.
steps.hint: Create a <div> to hold both the filter input and the table. The input should be a standard HTML input element.
steps.analogousExample: // Adding a container with input and table
steps.expectedOutcome: A container div appears below the heading, containing a filter input field and an empty table element.
successCriteria: The return statement includes a <div> container after the heading, with an <input> element (placeholder='Filter by name...') and an empty <table> element inside it.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some structure, but make sure to include both the input (with placeholder) and the empty table inside the container div.
steps.feedbackWrong: The container, filter input, or table is missing. Check that you've added a <div> after the heading containing both elements.

steps.title: Wire filter input to handleFilter function
steps.instruction: Add an onChange event handler to the filter input element that calls handleFilter with the input's current value.
steps.hint: Use the onChange prop on the input element and pass event.target.value to handleFilter.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: wiring an input to a handler
<input onChange={(e) => handleChange(e.target.value)} />
steps.expectedOutcome: The filter input will now call handleFilter whenever the user types, updating the filteredData state.
successCriteria: The input element has an onChange handler that calls handleFilter with the input value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the onChange handler calls handleFilter with the input's value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The filter input needs an onChange handler that calls handleFilter with the input value.

steps.title: Add table headers with sort buttons
steps.instruction: Inside the return statement of your component, add a <table> element with a <thead> containing table headers for 'ID', 'Name', and 'Age'. Each header should be a <th> with a button inside that calls handleSort with the appropriate key when clicked.
steps.hint: Create a table structure with headers that have clickable buttons. The button text should match the column name, and the onClick handler should call handleSort with the column key (e.g., 'id', 'name', 'age').
steps.analogousExample: // Example: Table headers with sort buttons
steps.expectedOutcome: A table structure with headers for ID, Name, and Age appears below the filter input. Each header has a button that, when clicked, will trigger the sorting logic for that column.
successCriteria: The table has a <thead> with three <th> elements containing buttons for 'ID', 'Name', and 'Age'. Each button's onClick handler calls handleSort with the correct key ('id', 'name', 'age').
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some table headers, but check that all three columns (ID, Name, Age) are present and each button calls handleSort with the correct key.
steps.feedbackWrong: The table headers with sort buttons are missing or incomplete. Make sure to add a <table> with <thead> containing <th> elements that have buttons with onClick handlers calling handleSort.

steps.title: Display filtered data in table rows
steps.instruction: Map through filteredData to create table rows with cell data inside the table body.
steps.hint: Use the map method on filteredData to generate <tr> elements, each containing <td> cells for id, name, and age.
steps.expectedOutcome: The table body will display rows with id, name, and age data from filteredData.
successCriteria: Table rows are generated using filteredData.map, each row has a unique key prop and contains <td> cells for id, name, and age.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but ensure you're using filteredData.map and including all three data fields in cells.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try mapping filteredData to create <tr> elements with <td> cells for id, name, and age inside the table body.

steps.title: Add visual sort indicators
steps.instruction: In your table headers, add conditional rendering to display up/down arrows based on the current sort direction for each column.
steps.hint: Check if sortConfig.key matches the column key, then show '↑' for ascending or '↓' for descending.
steps.analogousExample:
// Conditional arrow display
const arrow = sortConfig.key === 'name' ? (sortConfig.direction === 'asc' ? '↑' : '↓') : '';
steps.expectedOutcome: Each table header button will show a visual arrow indicator when that column is sorted, with up arrow for ascending and down arrow for descending.
successCriteria: The ID, Name, and Age header buttons display '↑' when sorted ascending, '↓' when sorted descending, and no arrow when not sorted.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added some indicators, but check that all three columns show arrows correctly based on sortConfig.
steps.feedbackWrong: The arrows aren't appearing correctly. Make sure you're comparing sortConfig.key with each column key and checking sortConfig.direction.
